extracted.intended_audience: regulatory agencies, lawmakers, attorneys general, advocacy groups, campaign vendors/lead_generators, and policymakers involved in notice-and-comment processes
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and recommended reforms for managing, validating, and policing public comments and mass submissions to government rulemakings and legislative advocacy (notice-and-comment systems), aimed at preventing fraud, impersonation, and astroturfing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mandate Disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Intermediaries should be required to disclose, with each comment or message submitted, the intermediary’s own identity and the identities of any parties that assisted in the generation or submission of the comments and messages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclosure could be in the text of a comment or in viewable metadata attached to the comment (e.g., “This comment was solicited and submitted by Company A, on behalf of Non-Profit X.”) and must be available to the public as part of any public comment process. Agencies should require advocacy groups and not just vendors to be identified. GSA's Regulations.gov API identity-validation model is a useful starting point but agencies must extend disclosure requirements to sponsorship and vendor chains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require express, informed consent before submitting on someone's behalf
rubrics_metrics.description: Advocacy groups and their vendors must obtain valid, express, informed consent from an individual before submitting a comment or message to the government on their behalf.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Settlements with lead generators require robust disclosures to consumers and prohibit submission of a comment or message on a consumer’s behalf unless the consumer has provided express, informed consent. This is intended to prevent impersonation and the use of consumers' names/addresses without authorization (e.g., co-registration fraud).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hold intermediaries to account for fake submissions
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should impose consequences on advocacy groups and vendors that submit fake comments or messages, placing responsibility on parties best positioned to detect and prevent fraud.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences may vary based on number of fake submissions attributable to the intermediary, whether submissions were inadvertent or intentional, and what preventive measures were in place. Possible sanctions include suspension of submission privileges and other administrative consequences. This shifts incentives away from volume-focused, low-quality lead-generation practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impose meaningful civil penalties and empower state attorneys general
rubrics_metrics.description: Laws and agency rules should provide for substantial civil fines and enforcement mechanisms that make fraud costly and not merely a cost of doing business; state attorneys general should be expressly authorized to enforce these statutes where residents’ information is misused.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Penalties should be scaled to deter mass impersonation and deception. Settlements described in the report include monetary penalties and reform obligations; legislative changes should provide comparable civil remedies and enforcement authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibit deceptive and unauthorized comments by statute
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress and state governments should prohibit knowingly submitting, or causing to be submitted, two or more comments or messages to the government (a) that are intended to deceive or (b) on behalf of someone else without first using reasonable measures to verify authorization via express, informed consent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A federal or state law would require advocacy groups to confirm valid consent before submitting comments and would prohibit submissions using fictitious identities intended to deceive. The law should include meaningful penalties and allow state AG enforcement. Anonymous comments signed 'anonymous' should not be penalized per privacy considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strengthen impersonation laws for mass impersonation
rubrics_metrics.description: Impersonation statutes should be amended to provide substantial penalties when many individuals are impersonated before a government agency or official.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Existing general impersonation and false-statement statutes were not designed to deter large-scale misuse of identities in comment dockets; legislatures should adjust penalties and scope to address mass impersonation in notice-and-comment contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implement technical safeguards against automated/bulk submissions
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies that accept electronic comments should implement technical measures to detect, limit, and mitigate automated or bulk submissions made by software or bots.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CAPTCHA is a recommended first step but is insufficient alone. Agencies should consider a layered approach including CAPTCHA, rate limiting, IP monitoring, traffic heuristics, and third-party bot-detection services. Technical safeguards should balance preventing automated abuse with preserving public access and not unduly burdening legitimate commenters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require registration and identity-validation for mass/API submitters
rubrics_metrics.description: Entities seeking to submit comments en masse via APIs or automated channels should be required to register and have their identities validated (as GSA currently does for Regulations.gov API users).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identity-validation provides a traceable record of who is submitting mass comments and facilitates accountability and investigations. Agencies should make registration metadata available to the public where appropriate and apply API controls to limit abuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make disclosure metadata publicly available for tracing and oversight
rubrics_metrics.description: Information about who solicited or submitted a comment (intermediary identity and sponsoring organizations) should be visible to the public to facilitate journalistic and public oversight and investigations into abuses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public availability of metadata helps the press and public identify astroturfing and hidden sponsors. Metadata disclosure can be embedded in the comment or attached as viewable metadata fields in the docket system.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require advocacy groups to disclose sponsorship and vendor relationships
rubrics_metrics.description: Campaign sponsors (advocacy groups) should disclose their role and any vendors used in solicitations so that the public and agencies know who is behind campaigns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclosing sponsorship prevents industry actors from hiding behind non-profits to create the false appearance of grassroots support (astroturfing). This should be required in solicitations, in comment text/metadata, and in any public-facing campaign materials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monitor subcontractors and retain records for accountability
rubrics_metrics.description: Campaigns that generate and submit comments must carefully monitor subcontractors and retain records to ensure oversight and facilitate investigations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Settlements require retention of records and monitoring; agencies should require similar recordkeeping and allow audits. This helps trace provenance of leads and detect fabricated consent or reuse of stale or breached data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibit submission-on-behalf where consent cannot be verified
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies and campaign sponsors should not allow submission of comments or messages purportedly from individuals where consent cannot be demonstrated or verified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This addresses co-registration fraud where vendors copied previously collected names/addresses or reused breached data. Systems should require evidence of an individual's current, informed opt-in prior to submission on their behalf.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve ability to submit anonymous comments while guarding against abuse
rubrics_metrics.description: Reforms should not foreclose anonymous comments; anonymous submissions that do not intend to deceive should remain permitted, but processes must include protections against fraud.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The report recognizes privacy and legitimate reasons for anonymity and recommends technical and procedural safeguards that protect anonymity while detecting mass automated or deceptive submissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide agencies authority and resources to adopt and implement reforms
rubrics_metrics.description: Legislatures should give agencies the authority to adopt recommended reforms and the resources needed to implement them uniformly and consistently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Without statutory authority and funding, agencies may lack the capacity to deploy technical defenses, enforce disclosure rules, or validate identity. Public-private partnerships can help where budgets are limited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encourage public-private partnerships for technical defenses
rubrics_metrics.description: Where budget shortfalls preclude government funding for new technologies, civic-minded private sector actors should partner with government to implement anti-abuse technologies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Private sector partners can supply bot-detection, rate-limiting, CAPTCHA, and other services to agencies lacking funds, but partnerships should preserve independence, transparency, and privacy protections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scale consequences to the scope, intent, and preventive measures taken
rubrics_metrics.description: Agency consequences for fraudulent submissions should consider (1) how many fake submissions are attributable to the intermediary, (2) whether submissions were inadvertent or intentional, and (3) what pre-existing measures the intermediary instituted to prevent fraud.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This principle supports proportional enforcement: negligent or unmonitored vendors can be sanctioned more heavily when they failed to implement reasonable safeguards; intentional fraud warrants stronger penalties and criminal referral where appropriate.
